lignes.texte: The AI job-pocalypse happened… you just weren’t paying attention.
Instead of the white collar cull, corporate leaders took a more surgical approach. They didn’t
lay off the veteran workers, they weaponized them with AI to multiply their workloads. Then they
slammed the door shut on everyone else. Entry jobs are being systematically wiped out and an entire
generation is being left of the sidelines.. The corporate ladder isn’t broken.
It’s being pulled up from the top. For decades, the path into a comfortable
middle-class life followed a familiar formula. Study hard, get a degree and pay your dues by
doing the grunt work. Entry level jobs were never meant to be glamorous. They were the tasks no
one else wanted to do: write boilerplate code, fill in spreadsheets or admin work. In exchange,
it was a foot in the door. New workers did the boring background work and got
to watch their more experienced colleagues and cultivate the soft skills to succeed.
It was the golden ticket. Now AI has torn it up.
Companies eliminated the need to hire and educate entry-level workers,
without having to put senior employees at any great risk. In fact, senior employees are
becoming more productive than ever before. Their lives are getting easier with AI on their side,
while the white collar workforce is locked out. And you only have to look at the front lines of
the tech industry to see the real, human cost of this trend. Graduates who did everything right,
and racked up 6 figure student loans, are being stonewalled. They’re getting
rejected daily… and not by HR departments, but by algorithms minutes after applying.
AI is soaking up the entry level roles and now graduates are fighting
over a shirking pool of jobs. And researchers at MIT wanted to
find out who was getting hit the hardest. To do that, they came up with something
called the “Iceberg Index”. It measures how much human work AI can actually do, based on
the specific skills required to do that work. The research team mapped over 32,000 distinct
work skills across 923 occupations and looked at how much overlap there was. They
found that AI was perfectly optimized to steal entry-level jobs. That’s because the knowledge
needed to carry out those tasks can be found in instruction manuals, textbooks, academic courses,
and operating procedures. It’s the same sources that make up a large portion of AI training data.
Meanwhile, AI wasn’t anywhere near as capable of taking on the types of tasks that more experienced
employees do in their day-to-day routines. Those are the tasks that rely on skills,
habits, and instincts picked up and honed over time. For example, in the legal industry,
AI can handle entry-level jobs like drafting legal summaries, but it can’t predict how a
judge will respond to a certain argument. So, senior employees don’t necessarily need
to worry about their job security. Their skills and knowledge are still needed.
They can happily embrace AI and enjoy the upsides without any of its downsides. That’s
why countless senior professionals are using AI assistants rather than junior associates
to handle parts of their daily workloads. In the law firms, the majority of senior
partners are using AI to claw back 20% of their week. Software engineers are getting work done
30% quicker thanks to AI. When more experienced workers embrace AI, it doesn’t take their jobs
from them; it makes them more effective. Why pay someone to do the boring tasks when
an AI agent can do it quicker, more efficiently and cheaper?
The business world is all about profit after all. It wasn’t that these companies wanted to close
the door on graduates. They needed to operate on economic logic. And economic
logic said that either reducing or freezing entry-level hiring was the smartest move.
So that’s what a lot of companies in the most AI-exposed sectors did.
And it’s created a paradox. On the surface everything looks fine. Unemployment numbers
are stable, senior staff are more efficient and executives are boasting about record
profits. But once you dig deeper, an entire tier of the workforce is being deleted.
And it isn’t sustainable. If companies stop hiring junior staff,
where are the leaders of tomorrow going to come from? When the executives, managers, and partners
decide to retire, who will take their place? Entry-level jobs were never just about doing
trivial or basic tasks. They were training grounds where graduates entered with nothing
but raw academic knowledge and transformed that into real-world business acumen.
Corporate leaders don’t seem to understand that. Or, they don’t care enough.
Either way, it’s a recipe for disaster. MIT researchers applied their Iceberg Index to
151 million workers across America. And the results were terrifying.
11.7% of the workforce can be replaced by AI right now.
That’s a wage bill of $1.2 trillion that machines can fill… a sum larger than the
entire gross domestic product (GDP) of developed nations such as Poland and Switzerland. This isn’t
some sort of hypothetical dystopian future. It’s happening right now. And as these models develop,
that number is only going to rise. But if such a large part of the US wage
bill could already be handled by machines, why hasn’t unemployment skyrocketed across the board?
The answer to that boils down to two important economic mechanisms,
known as “crashing waves” and “rising tides.” A crashing wave is typically defined as some
sort of sudden breakthrough that completely renders a human task or profession obsolete.
A cure for cancer would be a crashing wave, or an autonomous driving system that immediately
replaces millions of commercial drivers. With a crashing wave, the impact is instant.
And there are crashing waves in AI. They’re the ones being felt in the most
exposed fields, like translation. Clients are choosing to feed documents and audio files into
AI. It’s a similar story in copywriting, companies are asking ChatGPT or Claude to
generate their user manuals, blogs, and product descriptions, rather than experienced writers.
But, across the majority of the economy, AI isn’t acting like a crashing wave. It’s more like a
rising tide, and that’s something very different. Rising tides are much more gradual in terms of
how they take hold. It can take years for their full effects to be felt,
and their influence moves so slowly, you might not even notice it.. at least at first.
Take smartphones. They went from a niche luxury to an essential tool in a decade. Landlines were
wiped out and the way humans communicated was fundamentally altered. It’s a similar story
with streaming services. From starting out as a quirky alternative, they eventually killed
physical media. Now people juggle multiple subscriptions without a second thought.
Even though the end result of rising tides can be just as dramatic as crashing waves,
the change happens much more slowly and makes it easier for people to digest. It
gives them time to adapt, which means it doesn’t seem quite as scary or stressful.
AI is on a similar trajectory. But it’s not coming for your entertainment.
Sure, it’s not going to wipe out entire job categories overnight. And it’s not
triggering large-scale layoffs or shrinking payrolls at scale.
In fact, a recent study co-authored by MIT Sloan associate professor Lawrence Schmidt
found that firms that embraced AI experienced 6% higher employment growth. They also say a 9.5%
sales growth over a 5-year period compared to competitors that didn’t do the same.
Based solely on those numbers, it’s easy to make the argument that AI isn’t some
sort of job-killing monster machine, but a productivity aid. Something that helps
firms reach unprecedented levels of efficiency and optimization.
But there’s a darker side to that story. Because, while AI-adopting companies may
be expanding, that expansion isn’t evenly distributed. It’s mainly focused on senior
members of staff, who are becoming valuable assets. An experienced financial analyst who
used to spend the majority of their week compiling data and only a small percentage analyzing it,
can hand-off the compilation to AI and spend more time on analysis and
strategy. This can help them extract more valuable insights at a more rapid rate.
And because these kinds of workers are doing better than ever, so are their companies.
They’re making more money, which can help them hire more senior employees, increase salaries,
or expand into other regions. But all those benefits came at a cost, and the bill was sent
to those at the bottom: the entry-level workers who are seeing fewer opportunities come their way.
We’ve seen this kind of scenario play out before, where a new technology or
innovation truly transforms the working world. When automated teller machines, or ATMs,
were introduced in the 1970s, 400,000 of them rolled out across America over the
course of the following 4 decades. Early on in that process, people predicted that the
days of the bank teller were all but over. In reality, bank tellers didn’t disappear.
Their roles just changed. ATMs helped to reduce the
operating costs of banks, which allowed more branches to open. Tellers shifted
away from manually counting money to other duties, like helping customers with financial
products or handling queries and concerns. For a more recent and relevant example, in 2016,
the computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, nicknamed the “Godfather of AI”, said that medical schools
should stop training human radiologists. He beloved deep learning algorithms would be able to
do their work much more efficiently within a few years’ time, rendering the entire role obsolete.
10 years later, radiology departments still exist. In fact, at the Mayo Clinic, the radiology staff
has grown by 55%. These people haven’t lost their jobs to AI,
they’ve just seen their jobs augmented by AI. So, if this cycle has played out before,
why should people be worried about generative AI’s increasing capabilities?
Because this current “rising tide” is very different to those that have come before.
Previous technological waves may have transformed fields like banking and manufacturing, but they
still left enough room for the entry-level worker to get their foot in the door. When
ATMs were introduced, banks still needed to employ workers to liaise with customers.
The rise of generative AI is the first ever example of a new innovation that actively targets
and cannibalizes the kind of apprentice-level roles reserved for young, aspiring professionals.
A recent Stanford survey revealed 20% of workers feel that there’s a realistic risk
of them losing their job to generative AI within the next couple of years. This intense anxiety
is prevalent among the younger generations who are growing up with an unprecedented level of
uncertainty regarding their career prospects. This has led to some striking trends emerging
in the education sector, as students become much more cautious and selective about which
subjects they choose to study. The majors that were once seen as “golden tickets”
are being treated with fear and suspicion. At MIT, enrollment in computer science courses
has dropped by around 18%. The “Fundamentals of Programming” course - which was once hugely
popular and had close to 600 students as recently as spring of 2023 - now has less than 200.
Young adults are looking at the job market, and realizing that the old rules no longer apply.
Even something as simple as picking a major feels like spinning a roulette wheel, with a
50/50 chance of success or failure. Students know that one wrong move could ruin their professional
prospects, and paths that once seemed safe to tread are increasingly fraught with danger.
They’re being asked to commit years of their lives to obtain qualifications that might not
actually provide them with any benefits. And those in comfortable senior roles have
responded to this emerging crisis by telling students to simply “study AI.”
They usher them into AI-oriented courses and tell them to learn the
likes of “prompt engineering” and “AI strategy development.” But even these kinds of courses
aren’t guaranteed to lead to successful careers. Because even if a young person understands how to
write prompts effectively, they still don’t have the broader industrial knowledge and experience
they need to use those skills effectively. This is why the decision by an increasing number of
corporate leaders to stop hiring entry-level workers has effectively placed a ticking time
bomb at the heart of the American economy. Boardrooms and shareholders may be celebrating
today as their short-term margins explode, but they are throwing away
the future of their companies without even realizing it. In just a few years,
these same companies will need to start looking for intermediate employees - mid-career managers
or team leaders with a strong understanding of the operational realities of their
industries - but they won’t be able to find them. And they’ll only have themselves to blame.
Because they are pulling up the ladders and slamming the doors in the faces of
the eager graduates and entry-level employees who used to become those intermediate workers.
They are creating a talent vacuum, forcing extremely passionate, enthusiastic,
and hard-working young people to give up on their professional dreams. They are pushing students
away from studying important subjects, like computer science and data analysis,
because they’re frightened of not having any job prospects by the time they graduate.
The white collar job market has changed, and the era of receiving a comfortable starting wage to
perform administrative tasks is all but over. It’s students who are paying the price today,
but an even bigger bill is heading the way of those higher up the food chain…
It just might take a few more years to arrive. The arrival of AI has shattered the jobs market.
But the scare stories in the mainstream media aren’t true. The reality is much worse. Watch “AI
Isn’t Taking Your Job. The Reality Is WORSE” to find out how bad it really is. Or click on this.
